Corvin flew into the Stormwall and didn't get in the lifeboat. Hal Merrow's last log said she sent him away so he'd live to be brave about something else. He says it turns out to be us. He said it was raining on him specifically.
It is cold here. It is like being inside a closed eye.
Stay close. All of you. I don't like how quiet it is.
It is not quiet. Listen.
_Cass? Cass, the lamp's gone out. It's so dark._
That is her voice. My voice. Hers.
_Don't let go of my hand. Don't let go. Cass, you're hurting—_
He was holding on very tightly.
_FATHER! Father, Lysa's still out there! Leave the lamp! FATHER!_
That is him. He was twelve.
_...Cass? I can't see you. It's alright. I'll wait. I'm good at waiting._
She has been waiting for forty years.
A bedroom, made of memory. A small bed. A shelf of wooden animals. A girl of ten in a white dress, sitting on the end of the bed swinging her feet.
Oh! You have my face.
It looks good on you. You're older. I always wanted to be older.
I am sixteen. Or I appear so.
I was going to be sixteen. I had plans. I was going to be a sky-pilot. And a baker. Both.
Both is allowed. I am learning that.
Is Cass sad?
Yes. Very. He is trying to bring you back. He has built a whole noon for you to live in.
I know. I can hear him. He sings all the time. It's very loud. It's always the same song.
Will you tell him something for me?
Tell him I'm not in the noon. I'm not anywhere. I'm just a memory he's holding too tight. Memories don't grow up. People do.
And tell him he was a good brother. Tell him the lamp going out wasn't his fault. He always thinks everything's his fault.
I will tell him.
Lysa pulls the ribbon out of her hair and holds it out.
Here. For you. Not because you're me. Because I want somebody to wear it somewhere I never got to go.
Will you get old? Properly old? With wrinkles and everything?
I would like that very much.
Good. Do it for both of us.
The dark at the edges of the room thickens. Everything the Gloam has ever kept, every forgotten thing, leaning in — wanting one thing more.
_You are made of us. Come home. Be no one again._
No. I have a name. And now I have a present. You cannot have either.
I am keeping it. Not as Lysa. As someone who was given a present.
I know. I have decided to be a little vain about it. Pip says it is good for me.

Under Thornwood's roots we met Lysa — what's left of her. She gave Sable her ribbon and asked her to get old, properly old, for both of them. She gave her a message for Cassian. Sable says she'll deliver it.
Visitors! Mind the brass. Don't mind the biscuits. Take two, they're mostly raisins.
On the old woman's desk, under the biscuit tin, a brass nameplate: OTTOLINE MARSH, ASTRONOMER.
Ottoline Marsh— you wrote _The Sunward Atlas_!
Somebody READ it? Ha! That's both my readers in one week!
Cassian gave me a copy. Before— everything.
...Oh. Well. He always did have excellent taste in books, and dreadful taste in absolutely everything else.
When the sun broke, the stars came loose too. Only little ones. Starfall. They fell where the light was strongest — into the Lantern ruins, mostly, and the old sea floor.
I'm rebuilding my chart of the sky so I can see what's coming. I need the fragments. Seven, if my sums are right, and they usually are, except when they aren't.
Bring me what you find. I have a great many things I don't need, and one thing I'd very much like to give to the right person.
The Drowned Stars
Ottoline Marsh needs seven Starfall Fragments — splinters of starlight that fell into the Lantern ruins and the Drowned Reef.
Look at that sky. Seven little lights where there were none. I'll name one after you. Something dignified. "Wren's Embarrassment."
It's still falling, you know. The one that didn't land. The telescope will show you, if you've the nerve.
No starfall yet? Try the old Lanterns. Stars always did like a lighthouse.
And something for your trouble. Don't argue. I'm old, I'm allowed.
Ottoline sets the last fragment into the great brass orrery. Seven small lights wink on across the dome, and the whole observatory hums like a held note.
There. The drowned stars, back where they belong. Or near enough.
You can't put the old sun back, you know. Nobody can. Not the Hierophant, not a hundred Keepers.
But stars are only suns that are very far away. Perhaps the trick isn't to mend the big one. Perhaps it's to make a small one, close by, that belongs to everybody.
...A small one.
It's only a theory. I've written it in the margins of my own book. Nobody reads the margins.
Now. The thing I wanted to give to the right person. It isn't a thing. It's a way of looking.
Read the sky. Bend fate a little, when it needs bending. Never more than a little. It sulks.
...Oh. Oh, dear. With the chart complete I can see it. One of them didn't land. It's still falling. Toward _us_.
